title: Collections, Property Wrappers, Result Builders & Macros
scopeHtml: Scope: Array/Dictionary/Set, higher-order functions, lazy, strings and Unicode, property wrappers, result builders, Swift macros, key paths, dynamic features.

notes.title: Baseline and the map of this topic
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Kotlin you live in List, Map, Set, Sequence, annotations, delegated properties (by), DSLs built with lambdas-with-receiver (Compose, buildList), KSP/KAPT annotation processing, and reflection. Swift covers the same ground with value-type collections, Sequence/Collection protocols, property wrappers, result builders, macros and key paths.

Baseline: Swift 6 language mode, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18 minimum, SwiftUI-first. Macros need Swift 5.9+ (Xcode 15); @Observable needs iOS 17. Anything newer is marked verify.

Android (Kotlin) iOS (Swift)
List<T>, MutableList<T> [T] (Array, always value type, let vs var)
Map<K,V> [K: V] (Dictionary)
Set<T> Set<T>
Sequence<T> / asSequence() Sequence, .lazy
by lazy, by Delegates.observable property wrappers (@Lazy-like, @State)
Compose @Composable + lambdas with receiver @ViewBuilder result builder
KSP / annotation processors Swift macros (@Observable, #Preview)
KProperty1<T, R> KeyPath<Root, Value>

Analogy, afterwards: this topic is the toolbox drawer under the workbench: arrays and dictionaries are the hammer and screwdriver; wrappers, builders and macros are the power tools that make SwiftUI feel like magic.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up "Swift Array is a value type" with "Swift Array is always copied". It uses copy-on-write.
  • Treating macros as runtime magic; they run at compile time and expand to source code.

notes.title: Array, Dictionary and Set internals
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Android, ArrayList is a reference type: two variables to the same list see each other's changes. val/var only controls the reference. In iOS, Array is a struct: let means the contents cannot change, and assigning copies logically.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
var a = [1, 2, 3]
var b = a          // logically a copy
b.append(4)
print(a)           // [1, 2, 3]
print(b)           // [1, 2, 3, 4]

let fixed = [1, 2, 3]
// fixed.append(4)   // compile error: let
val a = mutableListOf(1, 2, 3)
val b = a                  // same reference
b.add(4)
println(a)                 // [1, 2, 3, 4]

val c = a.toMutableList()  // explicit copy

Copy on write (CoW):

  • An Array is a small struct holding one pointer to a heap buffer (header: count, capacity, then elements). Copying the struct copies the pointer and bumps a reference count (cheap, O(1)).
  • On the first mutation, Swift checks isKnownUniquelyReferenced on the buffer. If it is shared, it copies the elements (O(n)) first. If unique, it mutates in place.
  • Dictionary and Set are also CoW hash tables. String is CoW too (for large strings).
  • Your own structs are only CoW if you build it (wrap a class and use isKnownUniquelyReferenced). A struct with an array field inherits CoW from the array.

Complexity table:

Operation Array Dictionary / Set
Index / lookup O(1) O(1) average
Append amortised O(1) (capacity doubles) O(1) average insert
Insert / remove in middle O(n) n/a
contains O(n) O(1) (Set)
Iteration order defined undefined, and randomised per process

Hash seeding: Swift randomises hashing per process launch (SipHash with a random seed) to defend against hash flooding, so Dictionary iteration order differs between runs. Never rely on it; use OrderedDictionary from the swift-collections package (Apple) when you need order, or sort keys.

Practical rules:

  • Call reserveCapacity(_:) before a big loop of appends.
  • array[i] on out-of-range traps: Fatal error: Index out of range. There is no getOrNull; write array.indices.contains(i) or an extension subscript.
  • ArraySlice (a[1...3]) shares the parent buffer and keeps the whole buffer alive (memory leak pattern if you store the slice). Convert with Array(slice).
  • Dictionary lookup returns an optional; dict[key, default: 0] += 1 is the idiomatic counter.
  • Elements of Set and keys of Dictionary must be Hashable. Synthesised for structs/enums whose members are Hashable.
  • Equality: == on arrays is element-wise (O(n)).

Real industry usage: Instagram/Airbnb feed models use arrays of identifiable structs; diffable data sources use Set/Dictionary for index lookups; swift-collections (Deque, OrderedSet, OrderedDictionary, Heap) is used when stdlib structures are not enough. A frequent production incident: accidental O(n^2) from array.contains inside a loop over 50,000 items, found in Instruments Time Profiler as a hot Sequence.contains.

Analogy: CoW is sharing a Google Doc link until someone edits: everyone reads the same copy, and the first editor silently gets their own duplicate.

Common interview traps.

  • "Are Swift collections thread safe?" No. Value semantics help, but concurrent mutation of one variable is a data race; Swift 6 strict concurrency flags it.
  • Saying a let array of class instances is immutable: the references are fixed, the objects they point to can still change.
  • Assuming Dictionary preserves insertion order (Kotlin LinkedHashMap does, Swift does not).
  • Holding an ArraySlice and wondering why memory is not freed.

notes.title: Sequence and Collection protocols
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Kotlin, Iterable<T> gives map/filter, Collection adds size, List adds indexing, and Sequence is the lazy variant. In Swift the hierarchy is protocols you can conform to.

Sequence                      makeIterator() -> IteratorProtocol, single pass allowed
  Collection                  multi-pass, indices, subscript, count
    BidirectionalCollection   index(before:), reversed() is O(1) view
      RandomAccessCollection  O(1) index offset (Array)
    MutableCollection         subscript set
    RangeReplaceableCollection  append / insert / remove (Array, String)
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct Countdown: Sequence {
    let start: Int
    func makeIterator() -> some IteratorProtocol<Int> {
        var n = start
        return AnyIterator {
            defer { n -= 1 }
            return n > 0 ? n : nil
        }
    }
}

for n in Countdown(start: 3) { print(n) }     // 3 2 1
let evens = Countdown(start: 10).filter { $0 % 2 == 0 }
class Countdown(val start: Int) : Sequence<Int> {
    override fun iterator(): Iterator<Int> = object : Iterator<Int> {
        var n = start
        override fun hasNext() = n > 0
        override fun next() = n--
    }
}

for (n in Countdown(3)) println(n)
val evens = Countdown(10).filter { it % 2 == 0 }

(some IteratorProtocol<Int> uses primary associated types, Swift 5.7+; verify that your toolchain accepts it, otherwise return AnyIterator<Int>.)

Why it matters:

  • Writing a generic function against Collection or Sequence instead of Array works for Array, Set, Dictionary, String, ranges and your own types.
  • Indices are not always Int. String.Index is opaque because characters have variable width. s[s.startIndex], s.index(after:).
  • Sequence.underestimatedCount, first(where:), prefix, dropFirst, zip, enumerated(), stride(from:to:by:), sorted(by:) (introsort replaced by a stable-in-practice algorithm since Swift 5, but stability is not documented as guaranteed), min(), max() come for free.
  • AsyncSequence is the async twin (for await). See also async/await note (06_C1).

Analogy: Sequence is a conveyor belt (you can only watch it go by), Collection is a shelf (you can look again and at any slot).

Common interview traps.

  • Iterating a single-pass Sequence twice (e.g. a network stream wrapper) and getting nothing the second time.
  • Using Int indices on String (compile error 'subscript' is unavailable: cannot subscript String with an Int).
  • Believing sorted is guaranteed stable.

notes.title: map, filter, reduce, compactMap and flatMap
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. The functional vocabulary is nearly identical. The traps are naming: Swift's compactMap is Kotlin's mapNotNull, and Swift's flatMap on collections is Kotlin's flatMap.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
let names = ["Ada", "Linus", "", "Grace"]

let lengths = names.map { $0.count }                       // [3, 5, 0, 5]
let nonEmpty = names.filter { !$0.isEmpty }
let total = lengths.reduce(0, +)
let ints = ["1", "x", "3"].compactMap { Int($0) }          // [1, 3]
let flat = [[1, 2], [3]].flatMap { $0 }                    // [1, 2, 3]
let grouped = Dictionary(grouping: names, by: { $0.first })
let byId = Dictionary(uniqueKeysWithValues: users.map { ($0.id, $0) })
let (adults, minors) = (users.filter { $0.age >= 18 }, users.filter { $0.age < 18 })
val names = listOf("Ada", "Linus", "", "Grace")

val lengths = names.map { it.length }
val nonEmpty = names.filter { it.isNotEmpty() }
val total = lengths.fold(0) { a, b -> a + b }
val ints = listOf("1", "x", "3").mapNotNull { it.toIntOrNull() }
val flat = listOf(listOf(1, 2), listOf(3)).flatten()
val grouped = names.groupBy { it.firstOrNull() }
val byId = users.associateBy { it.id }
val (adults, minors) = users.partition { it.age >= 18 }

Notes:

  • Shorthand $0, $1 replaces Kotlin it; for key paths, Swift 5.2+ lets you pass a key path as a function: users.map(\.name).
  • reduce(into:) mutates an accumulator and avoids O(n^2) copies when building a dictionary or array:
let counts = words.reduce(into: [String: Int]()) { $0[$1, default: 0] += 1 }
  • Plain reduce(0) { $0 + $1 } copying an array accumulator is O(n^2). Always use reduce(into:) for collections.
  • Missing from Swift's stdlib, present in Kotlin: partition, associateBy, chunked, windowed, sumOf. Use swift-algorithms (Apple package: chunks(ofCount:), windows(ofCount:), uniqued(), partitioned(by:)) or write extensions. sum is reduce(0, +).
  • flatMap with a closure returning an optional was deprecated; use compactMap.
  • Chaining map creates an intermediate array per step; use .lazy (next section) to avoid it for large data.
  • Optional and Result also have map/flatMap.
  • forEach cannot break or return from the enclosing function; use for ... in for that.

Real industry usage: JSON-to-model mapping (items.compactMap(Model.init)), building diffable snapshot data, analytics event batching with swift-algorithms chunks.

Analogy: map is a stamping machine changing every item; filter is a sieve; reduce is a funnel into one bucket; compactMap is a sieve and stamp that discards "nothing".

Common interview traps.

  • Using flatMap where compactMap is meant.
  • reduce with an array accumulator and no into: (quadratic).
  • forEach with return expecting early exit from the function.
  • Android vs iOS: Kotlin map on a Map returns a List; Swift Dictionary.map returns an array, while mapValues keeps a dictionary.

notes.title: Lazy sequences
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Kotlin collection chains (list.filter{}.map{}) are eager and create intermediate lists; you call asSequence() to make them lazy. Swift's switch is .lazy.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
let result = (1...1_000_000)
    .lazy
    .filter { $0 % 3 == 0 }
    .map { $0 * 2 }
    .prefix(5)
// Nothing computed yet. Forced by:
print(Array(result))     // [6, 12, 18, 24, 30]
val result = (1..1_000_000).asSequence()
    .filter { it % 3 == 0 }
    .map { it * 2 }
    .take(5)
    .toList()

How it works: .lazy returns LazySequence / LazyCollection; each operator wraps the previous with a new lazy type (LazyFilterSequence, LazyMapSequence). Elements are pulled one at a time through the whole chain on demand, so prefix(5) stops early. Pitfalls:

  • Closures re-run every time you iterate or index the lazy result (no caching). A lazy map with an expensive closure over a Collection can be recomputed on each subscript access.
  • Lazy chains have complicated compiler-generated types; store them as some Sequence<Int> or convert with Array(...) at the boundary.
  • For tiny arrays, eager is faster (no wrapper overhead). Measure with Instruments.
  • Lazy closures capture state; capturing self strongly and storing the lazy sequence can create retain cycles.
  • lazy var is a different feature: a stored property initialised on first access (like Kotlin by lazy, but not thread safe).

Real industry usage: image-grid prefetch lists, search over large local datasets, parsing large logs line by line (FileHandle.bytes.lines is AsyncSequence).

Analogy: eager is cooking all 1,000,000 meals before dinner; lazy is a chef cooking each dish only when a customer orders.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing lazy caches results; it does not.
  • Confusing lazy var (stored property) with .lazy (sequence adapter).
  • Expecting side effects inside lazy map to run immediately.

notes.title: Strings, Characters and grapheme clusters
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. A Kotlin/Java String is a UTF-16 array; length counts 16-bit code units, so an emoji can count as 2 and s[i] can split a character. A Swift String is a collection of Characters = extended grapheme clusters (what a human sees as one character), stored internally as UTF-8 since Swift 5.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
let flag = "🇮🇳"                    // 2 Unicode scalars, 1 Character
let family = "👨‍👩‍👧"               // 5 scalars (3 people + 2 joiners), 1 Character
let e = "e\u{0301}"                // e + combining acute, 1 Character
print(flag.count)                  // 1
print(flag.unicodeScalars.count)   // 2
print(flag.utf8.count)             // 8
print(e == "é")                    // true (canonical equivalence)
val flag = "🇮🇳"
println(flag.length)                      // 4  (UTF-16 code units)
println(flag.codePointCount(0, flag.length))  // 2
println(flag.toByteArray().size)          // 8
println("é" == "é")                 // false (code unit comparison)

Facts:

  • count is O(n) (it must walk the string to find grapheme boundaries). isEmpty is O(1).
  • Indexing uses String.Index, not Int: s[s.index(s.startIndex, offsetBy: 3)].
  • Four views: String (Characters), .unicodeScalars, .utf8, .utf16. Use .utf8 for byte processing and network, .utf16 when talking to NSString or NSRange APIs.
  • Interop bug class: NSRange and NSAttributedString ranges are UTF-16 based; converting with Range(nsRange, in: string) is the safe route. Using s.count as an NSRange length breaks on emoji.
  • Comparison: == uses canonical equivalence (composed vs decomposed accent are equal). localizedCompare, localizedCaseInsensitiveContains, caseInsensitiveCompare for user-visible text.
  • Multi-line literals """, raw strings #"..."#, interpolation "\(x)" and String(localized:) for localisation (Xcode String Catalogs, .xcstrings, Xcode 15+).
  • Swift 5.9+ interpolation can take a custom DefaultStringInterpolation extension; String(format:) still works through Foundation.

Substring

s.prefix(3), split, dropFirst return a Substring, which shares storage with the original (like ArraySlice). It is cheap but keeps the original string alive. Convert with String(sub) before storing long-term.

let line = "key=value"
if let eq = line.firstIndex(of: "=") {
    let key = String(line[..<eq])            // copy out of the slice
    let value = String(line[line.index(after: eq)...])
}

Both conform to StringProtocol; write APIs as func f<S: StringProtocol>(_ s: S) to accept both.

Real industry usage: chat apps (WhatsApp-style) truncating messages by Character count so they never cut an emoji in half; Twitter-style character counting uses grapheme clusters plus weighted rules; text-field validation in banking apps uses unicodeScalars.

Analogy: a Kotlin string is a row of beads where one emoji may be two beads; a Swift string is a row of bead-groups the way a human sees them.

Common interview traps.

  • "Why can't I write str[0]?" Variable-width characters make Int indexing O(n) and ambiguous.
  • Treating count as O(1) in a hot loop.
  • Slicing a huge file's text into Substrings and storing them (memory held).
  • Using NSRange(location: 0, length: s.count) with emoji: use s.utf16.count.

notes.title: Property wrappers
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Kotlin has delegated properties: var name by Delegates.observable(...), val x by lazy {}, and Compose var count by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }. Swift's equivalent is a property wrapper: a type annotated @propertyWrapper that stores the value and intercepts get/set.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
@propertyWrapper
struct Clamped<Value: Comparable> {
    private var value: Value
    private let range: ClosedRange<Value>

    init(wrappedValue: Value, _ range: ClosedRange<Value>) {
        self.range = range
        self.value = min(max(wrappedValue, range.lowerBound), range.upperBound)
    }

    var wrappedValue: Value {
        get { value }
        set { value = min(max(newValue, range.lowerBound), range.upperBound) }
    }

    var projectedValue: ClosedRange<Value> { range }   // exposed as $volume
}

struct Player {
    @Clamped(0...100) var volume = 50
}

var p = Player()
p.volume = 250           // stored as 100
print(p.$volume)         // 0...100
class Clamped(private val range: IntRange, initial: Int) : ReadWriteProperty<Any?, Int> {
    private var value = initial.coerceIn(range)
    override fun getValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>) = value
    override fun setValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>, value: Int) {
        this.value = value.coerceIn(range)
    }
}

class Player { var volume by Clamped(0..100, 50) }

Desugaring (this is what interviewers ask):

// @Clamped(0...100) var volume = 50   expands approximately to:
private var _volume = Clamped(wrappedValue: 50, 0...100)
var volume: Int {
    get { _volume.wrappedValue }
    set { _volume.wrappedValue = newValue }
}
var $volume: ClosedRange<Int> { _volume.projectedValue }

Rules and behaviour:

  • wrappedValue is required. projectedValue is optional and is accessed with $name.
  • The wrapper is stored as a hidden property named _name, so it takes real memory in the enclosing struct.
  • Can be applied to properties of structs, classes, local variables and function parameters (Swift 5.5+ for local; parameters via SE-0293).
  • Codable synthesis wraps _name: encoding a property with a wrapper writes the wrapped type's key only if the wrapper itself is Codable.

How SwiftUI wrappers are built:

Wrapper wrappedValue $ projected value Key idea
@State value Binding<Value> storage owned by the view graph, outside the struct
@Binding value Binding<Value> read/write reference to someone else's state
@Environment value from env n/a read-only key lookup
@AppStorage UserDefaults value Binding wraps UserDefaults
@Bindable (iOS 17) n/a gives $model.field bindings to an @Observable
@FocusState, @Query (SwiftData), @SceneStorage

@State works even though views are value types that are recreated constantly because State keeps a reference to storage that SwiftUI manages; the struct only holds a handle. Deep dive of invalidation is in the SwiftUI track (see also J2).

Older equivalents you will meet: @Published in ObservableObject (Combine publisher as projected value $name), @StateObject, @ObservedObject, @EnvironmentObject; replaced by @Observable + plain @State in iOS 17.

Real industry usage: @UserDefault("flag") wrappers in many apps; @Injected property wrappers for dependency injection in Resolver and Factory libraries; Point-Free's @Dependency in swift-dependencies; Firebase's @FirestoreQuery.

Limitations: wrappers can't be applied to lazy properties; a wrapped property in a class with strict concurrency needs the wrapper to be Sendable-safe; custom wrappers with side effects in init are executed at instance creation.

Analogy: a property wrapper is a bouncer on a door for a single property: every entry and exit passes through his rules, and he keeps a spare ticket ($) you can ask for.

Common interview traps.

  • "What is $count?" It is the projected value; for @State it is a Binding.
  • Believing @State stores data in the view struct. It stores a handle to external storage.
  • Expecting a property wrapper to work inside an enum (enums can't have stored properties).
  • Android vs iOS: Kotlin's by delegates receive a KProperty; Swift wrappers do not, but @propertyWrapper supports static subscript(_enclosingInstance:...) to access the enclosing object (underscored/unofficial, verify before relying on it).

notes.title: Result builders
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Compose, a @Composable lambda emits UI as a side effect through the compiler plugin. In Kotlin DSLs like buildList { add(1) } or html { div { } } you rely on lambdas with receiver. Swift's equivalent is a result builder: a type marked @resultBuilder that the compiler uses to rewrite a block of statements into function calls.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
VStack {
    Text("Hello")
    if showImage {
        Image(systemName: "star")
    }
    ForEach(items) { Text($0.name) }
}
Column {
    Text("Hello")
    if (showImage) {
        Icon(Icons.Default.Star, null)
    }
    items.forEach { Text(it.name) }
}

How @ViewBuilder works. The block above is rewritten to something like:

VStack(content: {
    let v0 = Text("Hello")
    let v1: Image? = showImage ? Image(systemName: "star") : nil   // buildIf / buildEither
    let v2 = ForEach(items) { Text($0.name) }
    return ViewBuilder.buildBlock(v0, v1, v2)     // TupleView<(Text, Image?, ForEach<...>)>
})

Builder methods you can implement:

Method Purpose
buildBlock(_:) combine statements into one value
buildExpression(_:) convert each expression (e.g. String -> Text)
buildOptional(_:) if without else
buildEither(first:) / buildEither(second:) if/else, switch
buildArray(_:) for ... in loops
buildLimitedAvailability(_:) #available checks
buildFinalResult(_:) last transformation

A tiny custom builder:

@resultBuilder
enum StringBuilder {
    static func buildBlock(_ parts: String...) -> String { parts.joined(separator: "\n") }
    static func buildOptional(_ part: String?) -> String { part ?? "" }
    static func buildEither(first: String) -> String { first }
    static func buildEither(second: String) -> String { second }
}

func lines(@StringBuilder _ content: () -> String) -> String { content() }

let text = lines {
    "Line 1"
    if Bool.random() { "Maybe line 2" } else { "Other" }
}

Consequences you can reason about:

  • Static typing, not a runtime tree. buildBlock is generic: SwiftUI used to have overloads for up to 10 children (TupleView up to 10) which is why a 11th sibling view used to fail to compile; Swift 5.9 variadic generics (parameter packs) removed that limit in newer SDKs (verify your SDK, iOS 17+ toolchains).
  • The compiler type-checks a whole result builder body as one expression, which is why giant body properties produce "the compiler is unable to type-check this expression in reasonable time". Fix: extract subviews, use @ViewBuilder computed properties.
  • if in a builder yields _ConditionalContent, which changes view identity: toggling the branch destroys and recreates state of the branch's views. Contrast .opacity(0) which keeps identity.
  • You cannot put arbitrary statements (print) in a result builder body, unless wrapped in let _ = print(...).
  • @ViewBuilder applied to a var body: some View is implicit on the View protocol requirement.

Other result builders in the wild: @SceneBuilder, @ToolbarContentBuilder, @CommandsBuilder, SwiftUI @TableColumnBuilder; Apple's RegexBuilder (import RegexBuilder); Swift @DictionaryBuilder in Vapor/Hummingbird; SwiftHTML-style libraries; Point-Free's swift-html and Parsing; Package.swift target lists via arrays.

Analogy: a result builder is a kitchen ticket printer: you write a list of dishes, and the machine converts it into a single structured order the kitchen (type system) understands.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking SwiftUI views are objects in a tree at runtime; they are lightweight value descriptions built by the builder and diffed.
  • if vs .opacity/.hidden: state loss differences.
  • Declaring more than 10 siblings in older SDKs; the standard answer is Group or extraction.
  • Android vs iOS: Compose uses a compiler plugin with positional memoisation; SwiftUI uses result builders plus structural identity.

notes.title: Swift macros
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Android uses annotation processors (KAPT, KSP) for Dagger/Hilt, Room and Moshi codegen: the processor reads annotated source and generates new files. Swift macros are similar in spirit, but they are source-to-source transformations run by the compiler, written in Swift using the SwiftSyntax library, and shipped in a separate compiler plugin executable.

Two flavours:

Kind Syntax Example
Freestanding #name(...) #Preview, #Predicate, #expect, #warning, #selector-like
Attached @Name @Observable, @Model (SwiftData), @Test, @Suite

Attached roles: @attached(member), peer, accessor, memberAttribute, extension, body.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
import Observation

@Observable
final class CartViewModel {
    var items: [Item] = []
    var isLoading = false
    @ObservationIgnored var cache: [Int: Item] = [:]
}
class CartViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(CartState())
    val state: StateFlow<CartState> = _state.asStateFlow()
}

What @Observable expands to (conceptually): for each stored property it adds a hidden _items storage, replaces items with a computed property whose getter calls access(keyPath:) on an ObservationRegistrar, and whose setter calls withMutation(keyPath:); it also adds @ObservationTracked/ObservationRegistrar members and conformance to Observable. In Xcode you can right click the macro and choose Expand Macro to see the generated code. SwiftUI's body runs inside an observation scope (withObservationTracking), so only properties actually read in body cause an invalidation. That is the main improvement over ObservableObject, where any @Published change re-rendered every observing view.

Key facts:

  • Macros run at compile time, in a sandboxed process; they cannot read arbitrary files or the network.
  • Macros cannot see types, only syntax; they can generate code but not inspect semantic type information (limited, verify for newer releases).
  • Third-party macros are Swift packages and Xcode asks the developer to trust each macro target the first time (a security prompt; CI needs -skipMacroValidation).
  • Build-time cost: SwiftSyntax compiles from source in some setups, hurting clean build times. Prebuilt SwiftSyntax support is newer (verify).
  • Debug: set breakpoints in expanded code; expand macros in the editor.
  • #Preview replaced PreviewProvider structs (Xcode 15). #Predicate builds SwiftData/Foundation predicates type-safely. @Model makes a SwiftData class persistable. Swift Testing is macro based (@Test, #expect captures sub-expressions for good failure messages).

Real industry usage: Point-Free's @Reducer, @DependencyClient, @CasePathable (TCA 1.x); Apple's @Observable, @Model; community macros like MemberwiseInit, swift-case-paths. Uber and Airbnb have explored macros to replace sourcery-style codegen (Sourcery was the earlier external generator).

Analogy: a macro is a tailor with a template: you pin a note to the cloth (the annotation) and the tailor sews extra pieces in before the compiler "wears" it.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing macros run at runtime or can swizzle behaviour.
  • Not knowing how to see the expansion (Expand Macro).
  • Forgetting the build setting that CI needs to trust macros.
  • Android vs iOS: KSP can inspect semantic types; Swift macros mainly see syntax.

notes.title: Key paths
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Kotlin has property references: User::name (a KProperty1<User, String>). Swift key paths are written \User.name and are values you can store, pass and compose, and they support writing when the property is mutable.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct User { var name: String; var address: Address }
struct Address { var city: String }

let namePath: KeyPath<User, String> = \User.name
let cityPath = \User.address.city              // composed path
let u = User(name: "Ada", address: Address(city: "London"))
print(u[keyPath: cityPath])                    // London

var user = u
let writable: WritableKeyPath<User, String> = \User.name
user[keyPath: writable] = "Grace"

let names = users.map(\.name)                  // key path as a function (Swift 5.2)
let sorted = users.sorted { $0[keyPath: \.age] < $1[keyPath: \.age] }
val namePath: KProperty1<User, String> = User::name
val u = User("Ada", Address("London"))
println(namePath.get(u))

val names = users.map(User::name)
val sorted = users.sortedBy(User::age)

Type family:

Type Capability
KeyPath<Root, Value> read
WritableKeyPath read/write on var roots
ReferenceWritableKeyPath write via class reference
PartialKeyPath<Root> value type erased
AnyKeyPath root and value erased

Key paths are checked at compile time (unlike string-based KVC "name"), work with value types, and can walk optionals (\User.address?.city). Swift 5.8+ supports key paths to subscripts and \.self. Key path literals in Swift 6 can capture only Sendable data; a KeyPath is Sendable (Sendable status in the stdlib: verify).

Where they appear: SwiftUI (.sorted(using: KeyPathComparator(\.name)), @Query(sort: \Item.date), Table columns), Combine assign(to: \.text, on: label) (legacy; the on: variant retains the object strongly, a known leak pattern), SwiftData sort descriptors, @dynamicMemberLookup forwarding, lenses in TCA (CasePath is the enum counterpart), Core Data NSSortDescriptor(keyPath:).

Legacy: Objective-C #keyPath(User.name) strings and KVO observe(\.state) on NSObject subclasses (needs @objc dynamic).

Analogy: a key path is a treasure-map arrow that says "from any User, go to address, then city" without holding a specific user.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing \User.name (key path) with User.name (an invalid reference unless static).
  • assign(to:on:self) in Combine leaking self (retain cycle).
  • Assuming key paths can reference methods; they only reference properties and subscripts.

notes.title: Dynamic features
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Kotlin supports reflection (::class.memberProperties), invoke operator overloading, and delegated properties. Swift is statically typed and has no general runtime reflection for calling arbitrary members. It offers targeted escape hatches.

@dynamicMemberLookup

Allows obj.anything to compile and route to a subscript(dynamicMember:). A type-safe variant takes a key path.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
@dynamicMemberLookup
struct Wrapper<T> {
    var value: T
    subscript<U>(dynamicMember keyPath: KeyPath<T, U>) -> U {
        value[keyPath: keyPath]
    }
}

let w = Wrapper(value: User(name: "Ada", address: Address(city: "London")))
print(w.name)          // forwards to value.name
class Wrapper<T>(val value: T) {
    // Kotlin: no equivalent; you write explicit delegation
    val name: String get() = (value as User).name
}

@Bindable and Binding use this so $model.title and $binding.field work, and Binding<Value> is @dynamicMemberLookup to project fields into sub-bindings.

@dynamicCallable

Makes obj(1, 2) callable via dynamicallyCall(withArguments:); used by Python interop (PythonKit) and some DSLs.

Mirror

Mirror(reflecting: value) gives read-only reflection of stored properties, used for debug printing and test helpers. It is slow and unsafe for logic.

Objective-C runtime

For NSObject subclasses marked @objc dynamic, you can use KVO, perform(_:), NSSelectorFromString, and method swizzling (Sentry, Firebase Analytics and older analytics libraries swizzle UIViewController.viewDidAppear). This is legacy-style but still found in production SDKs.

callAsFunction and others

func callAsFunction() lets an instance be called like a function, e.g. SwiftUI-style helpers such as AsyncImagePhase-like objects or Regex/DismissAction (@Environment(\.dismiss) var dismiss; dismiss()). subscript overloads, ExpressibleByStringLiteral, ExpressibleByArrayLiteral and ExpressibleByDictionaryLiteral let your types be created from literals.

Real industry usage: Sentry/Firebase/Instabug use swizzling; Realm and Core Data rely on @objc dynamic; Point-Free uses key paths and case paths for navigation state.

Analogy: Swift's dynamic features are emergency exits, clearly signed. The building (static typing) has no open windows, so you can't wander out by accident.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing Swift has full reflection like Java; Mirror is read-only and slow.
  • Swizzling in Swift code requires @objc dynamic; pure Swift methods are statically or vtable dispatched and cannot be swizzled.
  • Overusing @dynamicMemberLookup with string keys, which loses compile-time checking.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Swift collections are CoW value types: assigning is O(1), first mutation of a shared buffer is O(n); ArraySlice and Substring share storage and can retain memory.
  • Dictionary and Set order is undefined and randomised per launch; use OrderedDictionary from swift-collections when you need order.
  • Write generic code over Sequence / Collection; String indices are not Int because of variable-width grapheme clusters, and count is O(n).
  • map/filter/reduce/compactMap/flatMap mirror Kotlin; use reduce(into:) for collections and .lazy for large chains (lazy does not cache).
  • Property wrappers are wrappedValue + optional projectedValue ($); @State, @Binding, @Environment, @AppStorage are all built this way, and @Observable replaces @Published/ObservableObject on iOS 17+.
  • Result builders rewrite a block into buildBlock/buildEither/buildOptional calls; @ViewBuilder is why if changes view identity and why huge bodies slow type-checking.
  • Macros are compile-time source expansions (SwiftSyntax) used by @Observable, @Model, #Preview, Swift Testing; they need explicit trust in Xcode and CI.
  • Key paths are first-class typed property references; use them for sorting, bindings and @dynamicMemberLookup, and avoid Combine assign(to:on:self) retain cycles.
  • Unverified details: variadic-generic ViewBuilder limits per SDK, KeyPath Sendable status, prebuilt SwiftSyntax availability, primary associated type iterator syntax (verify).
